cards.title: Animals killed for food each year
cards.takeaway: Around 88 billion land animals were slaughtered for food in 2024, about 2,800 every second (FAOSTAT via Faunalytics, 2026). On top of that, around 124 billion farmed fish are killed each year (Mood et al., 2023), and an estimated 1.1–2.2 trillion wild fish are caught (Mood & Brooke, 2024).
cards.sayIt: "Every second, about 2,800 land animals are killed for food. That's 88 billion a year, over ten for every person on Earth. And that's before counting fish, which run to over a trillion."

cards.title: Male calves in the dairy industry
cards.takeaway: To produce milk, a cow must give birth, and about half her calves are male. Male calves of dairy breeds are of little use to the dairy industry: most are killed within days or raised for veal or beef. In New Zealand alone, about 2 million "bobby calves" are produced each year. Around 1.7 million are slaughtered at about 4 days old, and ~245,000 are killed on the farm (DairyNZ estimates, 2021). There is no reliable global count.
cards.sayIt: "Cows only make milk after giving birth, so dairy farms produce millions of calves they don't need. In New Zealand, around 1.7 million calves a year are sent to slaughter at just four days old."

cards.title: Male chicks culled by the egg industry
cards.takeaway: The egg industry kills an estimated 7.8 billion male chicks a year (2024), up from 7.1 billion in 2019. That's about 250 every second. Male chicks of egg-laying breeds can't lay eggs and grow too slowly to be raised profitably for meat, so they are killed within hours of hatching, usually by maceration (high-speed grinding) or gassing (Faunalytics, 2026).
cards.sayIt: "For every egg-laying hen, a brother chick was killed on his first day. That's nearly 8 billion male chicks a year, usually ground up or gassed. It happens on free-range and organic farms too, because they buy hens from the same hatcheries."

cards.title: Pigs stunned with carbon dioxide gas
cards.takeaway: In England and Wales, 90% of pigs are stunned before slaughter with high-concentration carbon dioxide (CO₂) (Food Standards Agency, 2024). Pigs are lowered in groups into a pit of CO₂, which the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and UK advisory bodies say is aversive and causes severe pain and distress before the animals lose consciousness. The UK's Animal Welfare Committee recommended phasing it out within five years (2025). It remains the standard method.
cards.sayIt: "Nine in ten pigs slaughtered in England and Wales are gassed with CO₂ first. The UK government's own advisers and the EU's food safety authority say it causes pigs severe pain and distress, yet it's still the industry standard."

cards.title: Share of farmed animals on factory farms
cards.takeaway: An estimated three-quarters (74%) of the world's farmed land animals live on factory farms: about 23 billion animals at any one time. Including farmed fish, it's about 94%. In the United States, over 99% of farmed animals are factory-farmed (Our World in Data, 2023, from Sentience Institute estimates).
cards.sayIt: "Most farm animals don't live on the farms people picture. About three-quarters of the world's farmed land animals are on factory farms, and in the US it's over 99%."

cards.title: Plant-based diets and heart disease
cards.takeaway: People eating vegetarian and vegan diets have about a quarter lower risk of ischaemic (coronary) heart disease than meat eaters: 25% lower in a pooled analysis of studies (Dinu et al., 2017) and 22% lower in a UK study of 48,000 people followed for 18 years (Tong et al., 2019). They also have lower body weight, cholesterol and blood sugar, and vegetarians have 8% lower total cancer incidence (vegans 15%). The same UK study found a 20% higher risk of stroke in vegetarians.
cards.sayIt: "Vegetarians and vegans have roughly a quarter lower risk of coronary heart disease than meat eaters, along with lower cholesterol and body weight. That's from large long-term studies."

cards.title: Processed and red meat and cancer
cards.takeaway: The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1): it causes bowel (colorectal) cancer. Red meat is classified as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A). Every 50 g of processed meat eaten daily raises bowel cancer risk by about 18% (IARC, 2015).
cards.sayIt: "The World Health Organization's cancer agency says processed meat like bacon, ham and sausages causes bowel cancer. Eating about 50 grams a day raises your risk by around 18%. Red meat is classed as a probable cause."

cards.title: Dietetic associations on plant-based diets
cards.takeaway: The British Dietetic Association states that "plant-based diets can support healthy living at every age and life stage", including childhood, pregnancy and breastfeeding, when well planned (BDA, 2021). The US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics says appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets "can be nutritionally adequate and can offer long-term health benefits" for adults (Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 2025).
cards.sayIt: "The British Dietetic Association, the professional body for UK dietitians, says a well-planned plant-based diet can support healthy living at every age and life stage. The main thing you need to add is vitamin B12."

cards.title: Getting key nutrients from plants
cards.takeaway: A varied plant-based diet can supply every nutrient people need except vitamin B12, which is made by bacteria and must come from fortified foods or a supplement. Protein needs are easily met from beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts and seeds. A few nutrients need some planning: iodine, omega-3, calcium, iron and zinc (British Dietetic Association, 2021).
cards.sayIt: "Plants cover everything except vitamin B12, which comes from bacteria, so vegans take a supplement or eat fortified foods. Protein is the easy part: beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and seeds."

cards.title: Animal farming and zoonotic disease
cards.takeaway: About 60% of known human infectious diseases and 75% of emerging ones come from animals. The UN Environment Programme names rising demand for animal protein and intensive, unsustainable farming among the seven main drivers of new outbreaks (UNEP, 2020). The 2009 swine flu pandemic, which originated in pigs in Mexico (Mena et al., 2016), killed an estimated 151,700–575,400 people in its first year (Dawood et al., 2012).
cards.sayIt: "Three-quarters of new infectious diseases come from animals, and the UN lists demand for animal protein and intensive farming among the main drivers. The 2009 swine flu pandemic came from pig farming and killed hundreds of thousands of people."

cards.title: Antibiotic use in farm animals
cards.takeaway: An estimated 73% of all antimicrobials sold worldwide are used in animals raised for food (Van Boeckel et al., 2019). Resistance in farm animals is rising fast: in low- and middle-income countries, the share of antibiotics that fail more than half the time nearly tripled in chickens and pigs between 2000 and 2018. Antibiotic-resistant infections directly killed 1.14 million people in 2021 and are forecast to kill 39 million between 2025 and 2050 (GRAM Project, 2024).
cards.sayIt: "Nearly three-quarters of the world's antibiotics are used on farm animals, not people. Resistant infections already kill over a million people a year, and overuse on farms is one of the things driving resistance."

cards.title: Agriculture's share of global emissions
cards.takeaway: Producing our food causes roughly a fifth to a third of all human greenhouse gas emissions, depending on what you count. Counting the whole food system, from farm and land clearing to processing, transport, retail and waste, it is about a third (32% in 2023).
cards.sayIt: "About a third of global emissions come from the food system, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization."

cards.title: Animal farming vs AI data centres
cards.takeaway: All the world's data centres (AI included) emit about 180 million tonnes of CO₂ a year, about 0.5% of global energy CO₂ (IEA, 2025). Livestock emit about 34 times as much (6.2 billion tonnes CO₂eq, FAO, 2023). Switching the world to plant-based diets would cut ~37 times more emissions than shutting down every data centre. On water, livestock's irrigation and drinking water alone is about 270 times data centres' total water consumption. 🧮
cards.sayIt: "If you're worried about AI's footprint, that's fair, but it's small next to what's on our plates. Livestock emit around 30 times more than all the world's data centres, and use hundreds of times more water."

cards.title: Livestock's share of global emissions
cards.takeaway: Raising animals for meat, milk and eggs causes about 12% of all human greenhouse gas emissions (FAO, 2023). Animal-based foods produce more than half (57%) of food-production emissions (Xu et al., 2021) while supplying under a fifth (18%) of the world's calories and just over a third (37%) of its protein (Poore & Nemecek, 2018).
cards.sayIt: "Livestock alone cause about 12% of global emissions. That's the latest estimate from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2023). Animal foods are over half of food's climate footprint but give us less than a fifth of our calories and just over a third of our protein."

cards.title: Agriculture's share of freshwater use
cards.takeaway: Farming is by far the largest user of fresh water. It takes about 70% of all freshwater withdrawn from rivers, lakes and aquifers (72% in FAO's latest data). Counting rainwater used by crops as well, agriculture makes up 92% of humanity's total water footprint (Hoekstra & Mekonnen, 2012).
cards.sayIt: "Around 70% of the fresh water we take from rivers and aquifers goes to farming. That's the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's figure (FAO, 2025). Industry and households share the rest."

cards.title: Animal products' share of agricultural water
cards.takeaway: Producing meat, dairy and eggs accounts for nearly a third of agriculture's total water footprint (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012), and over half if all water on grazing land is counted (Weindl et al., 2017). Most of this is rainwater, mainly for feed and pasture. Counting only irrigation water, animal products' share is much smaller (roughly a sixth).
cards.sayIt: "Nearly a third of farming's water footprint goes to animal products (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012). That's mostly rainwater on feed crops and pasture, so the bigger issue is how inefficiently animals turn that water into food."

cards.title: Water footprint of animal vs plant foods
cards.takeaway: For the same nutrition, animal foods need far more water than plant foods. Per calorie, beef's water footprint is about 20 times that of cereals and starchy roots. Per gram of protein, meat's footprint is 1.5 to 6 times that of pulses (beans, lentils, peas). The main reason is that animals turn only a small part of their feed into food (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012).
cards.sayIt: "Calorie for calorie, beef takes about 20 times more water than grains or potatoes. Even for protein, meat needs up to six times more water than beans or lentils (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012)."

cards.title: Agriculture and deforestation
cards.takeaway: Agriculture drives almost 90% of global deforestation. Livestock grazing alone accounts for 38.5% (FAO, 2022). In the tropics, cattle pasture is the single biggest driver, causing about 41% of tropical deforestation, more than palm oil and soy combined (Pendrill et al., 2019).
cards.sayIt: "Farming causes almost 90% of the world's deforestation, and grazing livestock alone account for nearly 40% of it. That's the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's own satellite survey (FAO, 2022)."

cards.title: Land saved by plant-based diets
cards.takeaway: If the world stopped eating meat and dairy, global farmland use could fall by more than 75%. That's an area about the size of the USA, China, the European Union and Australia combined, and the world would still be fed (Poore & Nemecek, 2018).
cards.sayIt: "If we all ate plant-based, we'd need over 75% less farmland. That frees up an area the size of the US, China, the EU and Australia put together, and we'd still feed everyone (Poore & Nemecek, 2018)."

cards.title: Land use of animal vs plant foods
cards.takeaway: For the same amount of protein, beef from beef herds needs about 164 m² of land per 100 g of protein. Peas need about 3.4 m²: roughly 50 times less. Even the lowest-impact beef uses about 36 times more land than peas (Poore & Nemecek, 2018).
cards.sayIt: "Getting your protein from beef takes about 50 times more land than getting it from peas. Even the most efficient beef farms use over 30 times more land (Poore & Nemecek, 2018)."

cards.title: Livestock's share of agricultural land
cards.takeaway: Farming covers almost half (44%) of the world's habitable land. About 80% of that farmland is used for livestock, as grazing land and cropland for animal feed. Yet meat, dairy and farmed fish supply only 17% of the world's calories and 38% of its protein (Ritchie & Roser, 2019, from FAO data).
cards.sayIt: "Around 80% of the world's farmland goes to raising animals, but they give us less than a fifth of our calories (Our World in Data, using UN Food and Agriculture Organization data)."

questions.ask: Roughly how many land animals were slaughtered for food worldwide in 2024?
questions.explain: FAOSTAT data compiled by Faunalytics: 87.9 billion land animals slaughtered in 2024, over ten for every person on Earth.

questions.ask: About how many land animals are slaughtered for food every second?
questions.explain: 88 billion a year ÷ 31.5 million seconds ≈ 2,800 per second, about 240 million a day.

questions.ask: What share of land animals slaughtered for food are chickens?
questions.explain: 78.5 billion chickens out of ~88 billion land animals in 2024. Cattle are only ~0.3%.

questions.ask: Roughly how many pigs are slaughtered worldwide each year?
questions.explain: FAOSTAT 2024: ~1.5 billion pigs, about 4.1 million per day.

questions.ask: Roughly how many wild fish are caught each year?
questions.explain: Mood & Brooke (Animal Welfare, 2024) estimate 1.1–2.2 trillion wild fish caught a year (2000–2019 average). About half go to fishmeal and fish oil, mostly animal feed.

questions.ask: Roughly how many farmed fish were killed for food in 2019?
questions.explain: Mood et al. (Animal Welfare, 2023): ~124 billion farmed fish killed in 2019, a nine-fold increase since 1990.

questions.ask: Why does the dairy industry produce large numbers of unwanted male calves?
questions.answer: Cows must give birth to produce milk, and about half the calves are male
distractors: Male calves are bred to guard the herd
Bulls are needed to produce milk
Male calves are needed for milk testing
questions.explain: Dairy cows are made pregnant about once a year. Males of dairy breeds are poor for beef, so most are killed young or raised briefly for veal or beef.

questions.ask: Roughly how many 'bobby calves' (surplus dairy calves) does New Zealand's dairy industry produce each year?
sourceDistractors: UK Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), 2025
questions.explain: DairyNZ estimates for 2020: ~2 million bobby calves, ~1.7 million sent to slaughter at about 4 days old, ~245,000 killed on farm.

questions.ask: At about what age are New Zealand bobby calves sent to slaughter?
questions.explain: New Zealand law requires calves to be at least 4 days old before transport to slaughter. Most go at 4–6 days.

questions.ask: By how much have dairy bull calf births in Great Britain fallen over the past decade, mainly due to sexed semen?
questions.source: UK Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), 2025
questions.explain: The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) reports a 65% fall. Sexed semen now makes up 84% of dairy semen sales.

questions.ask: Roughly how many male chicks does the egg industry kill worldwide each year?
questions.explain: Faunalytics (2026) estimates 7.83 billion in 2024, up from 7.08 billion in 2019. That's about 250 every second.

questions.ask: Why are male chicks of egg-laying breeds killed?
questions.answer: They can't lay eggs and grow too slowly to be profitable for meat
distractors: They carry diseases that threaten the hens
They are too aggressive to keep
It is required by food safety law
questions.explain: Laying breeds are bred for egg output. Males are economically 'surplus' and are killed within hours of hatching.

questions.ask: What are the two main methods used to kill male chicks?
distractors: They are released into the wild
questions.explain: The EU permits only maceration and gassing (CO₂ or inert gas). Maceration dominates in the US and Australia.

questions.ask: Does buying free-range or organic eggs avoid chick culling?
questions.answer: Generally no: hens come from hatcheries that cull their brothers
distractors: Yes, free-range farms keep all the males
Yes, organic rules ban culling worldwide
Yes, free-range hens are a breed with no male chicks
questions.explain: Only eggs from in-ovo sexing or brother-rearing schemes avoid it. That's standard only where culling is banned (Germany, Austria, France, and Italy from 2027).

questions.ask: Which country banned chick culling from 1 January 2022?
questions.explain: Germany banned it from 1 January 2022, followed by Austria (July 2022) and France (2023). Italy's ban applies from 2027. The US has no ban.

questions.ask: In England and Wales, what share of pigs are stunned with high-concentration carbon dioxide gas before slaughter?
sourceDistractors: UK Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), 2025
questions.explain: The Food Standards Agency's 2024 Slaughter Sector Survey found 90% of pigs were stunned with high-concentration CO₂. Most of the rest were stunned electrically.

questions.ask: What do the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and UK advisers say about high-concentration CO₂ stunning of pigs?
questions.answer: It is aversive and causes severe pain and distress before unconsciousness, and should be phased out
distractors: It is the most humane method available
It causes no distress because pigs can't smell CO₂
It is banned across the EU
questions.explain: Both have recommended phasing it out. In 2025 the UK Animal Welfare Committee proposed ending it within five years, which the industry opposes.

questions.ask: In England and Wales, roughly what share of meat chickens are gas-stunned before slaughter?
distractors: None: gas stunning is not used for poultry
questions.explain: The 2024 Food Standards Agency survey found ~77% of meat chickens were gas-stunned.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of the world's farmed land animals are estimated to live on factory farms?
questions.explain: Our World in Data (Ritchie, 2023), using Sentience Institute estimates: ~74% of farmed land animals, about 23 billion at any time. Over 99% is the US figure.

questions.ask: What share of farmed animals in the United States live on factory farms?
questions.explain: Sentience Institute's 2022 estimate from US agricultural census data: over 99% of US farmed animals, just over 10 billion, are factory-farmed.

questions.ask: Including farmed fish, roughly what share of farmed animals worldwide are factory-farmed?
questions.explain: Farmed fish are assumed to be almost all factory-farmed. With ~111 billion farmed fish alive at any time included, the share rises to ~94%.

questions.ask: What definition do factory-farming estimates usually rely on?
questions.answer: Concentrated animal feeding operations: confined 45+ days a year, no outdoor grazing, above a size threshold
distractors: Any farm with more than 10 animals
Farms owned by corporations rather than families
questions.explain: There's no universal legal definition. Estimates use the US concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFO) criteria.

questions.ask: Compared with meat eaters, roughly how much lower is the risk of ischaemic (coronary) heart disease in vegetarians and vegans?
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: Dinu et al.'s pooled analysis found 25% lower. The UK EPIC-Oxford study (Tong et al., 2019) found 22% lower over 18 years.

questions.ask: In the UK EPIC-Oxford study of 48,000 people, how did vegetarians' risk of stroke compare with meat eaters'?
questions.answer: 20% higher (about 3 more cases per 1,000 people over 10 years)
questions.explain: The same study found 10 fewer heart disease cases per 1,000 over 10 years. Concede the stroke finding and give both numbers.

questions.ask: How does total cancer incidence in vegans compare with meat eaters, in pooled studies?
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: Dinu et al. found total cancer incidence 8% lower in vegetarians and 15% lower in vegans.

questions.ask: Do pooled studies show that vegetarians and vegans have lower all-cause mortality (live longer)?
questions.answer: No: no significant difference was found
questions.explain: Dinu et al. (2017) found lower heart disease and cancer incidence, but no significant difference in all-cause mortality. Don't claim vegans live longer.

questions.ask: Which risk factors are significantly lower in vegetarians and vegans than in meat eaters?
questions.answer: Body mass index, total and LDL cholesterol, and blood glucose
distractors: Vitamin D and iron levels only
questions.explain: Dinu et al. pooled 86 cross-sectional studies and found all of these significantly lower.

questions.ask: How does the World Health Organization's cancer agency classify processed meat such as bacon, ham and sausages?
questions.source: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (2015) found sufficient evidence that processed meat causes colorectal cancer. Red meat is Group 2A, probably carcinogenic.

questions.ask: Which cancer does processed meat cause, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer?
questions.explain: The agency concluded that eating processed meat causes colorectal cancer. A link with stomach cancer was seen but isn't conclusive.

questions.ask: By about how much does eating 50 g of processed meat a day raise the risk of bowel cancer?
questions.source: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: Each 50 g daily portion raises colorectal cancer risk by about 18%, relative to your existing risk.

questions.ask: How is red meat (beef, pork, lamb) classified?
questions.explain: The evidence for red meat is limited but supported by strong mechanistic evidence, so it's 'probably carcinogenic'.

questions.ask: Processed meat is in the same group as tobacco. Does that mean it is as dangerous?
questions.answer: No: the group reflects how strong the evidence is, not how big the risk is
distractors: Yes: all Group 1 agents are equally dangerous
Yes: it causes as many deaths as smoking
questions.explain: Tobacco causes about 1 million cancer deaths a year. About 34,000 are attributed to diets high in processed meat.

questions.ask: What does the World Cancer Research Fund recommend for processed meat?
distractors: Up to 70 g a day is safe
No limit if it is organic
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: It also advises no more than about three portions of red meat a week (350–500 g cooked weight).

questions.ask: What does the British Dietetic Association say about plant-based diets?
questions.answer: They can support healthy living at every age and life stage
distractors: They are suitable for adults only
They are safe only under medical supervision
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: The British Dietetic Association's food fact sheet says: 'Plant-based diets can support healthy living at every age and life stage', when well planned.

questions.ask: Which life stages does the British Dietetic Association say a well-planned vegan diet can support?
questions.answer: All ages, including childhood, pregnancy and breastfeeding
questions.explain: Its statement with The Vegan Society says a balanced vegan diet can be enjoyed by 'children and adults, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding'.

questions.ask: What does the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics' 2025 position say about vegetarian and vegan diets for adults?
questions.answer: They can be nutritionally adequate and offer long-term health benefits
distractors: They are adequate only with meat substitutes
They raise the risk of heart disease
They should be limited to a few months
questions.explain: The 2025 position covers adults: appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets 'can be nutritionally adequate and can offer long-term health benefits'.

questions.ask: How does the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics' 2025 position differ from its 2016 one?
questions.answer: The 2025 position covers adults only; 2016 covered all stages of life
distractors: The 2025 position advises against vegan diets
questions.explain: The 2025 paper doesn't address pregnancy or childhood. For 'every age and life stage', quote the British Dietetic Association instead.

questions.ask: Which nutrient can't be obtained from plants, so must come from fortified foods or a supplement on a vegan diet?
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: B12 is made by bacteria, not plants or animals. The British Dietetic Association says vegans' only reliable sources are fortified foods and supplements.

questions.ask: Where does vitamin B12 originally come from?
questions.explain: Neither plants nor animals make B12. Bacteria do.

questions.ask: What does the British Dietetic Association say about meeting protein needs on a plant-based diet?
questions.answer: They are easily met from beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts and seeds
distractors: They can only be met by combining foods at every meal
They can't be met without eggs or dairy
questions.explain: The fact sheet lists lentils, beans, chickpeas, seeds, nuts, nut butters, tofu and tempeh as good sources.

questions.ask: What improves the absorption of iron from plant foods?
questions.answer: Eating them with vitamin C, e.g. citrus fruit, berries or peppers
distractors: Taking calcium at the same time
questions.explain: Plant (non-haem) iron is absorbed less efficiently than the haem iron in meat. Vitamin C improves absorption.

questions.ask: What is a vegan source of the long-chain omega-3 fats found in oily fish?
questions.explain: Fish get long-chain omega-3 from algae. Walnuts, flaxseeds, chia and hemp seeds supply the shorter form, which the body converts.

questions.ask: Besides B12, which nutrient does the British Dietetic Association flag as a deficiency risk on exclusively plant-based diets, because its main sources are dairy and seafood?
questions.explain: Options are iodine-fortified plant milks or seaweed no more than once a week. Too much iodine is also harmful.

questions.ask: What is the difference between haem and non-haem iron?
questions.answer: Haem iron is only in animal flesh and is absorbed more readily; non-haem iron is the form in plants
distractors: Haem iron is the form in plants; non-haem is in meat
Non-haem iron can't be absorbed at all
They are two names for the same thing
questions.explain: Plants contain only non-haem iron, which is absorbed less efficiently. Vitamin C helps.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of emerging infectious diseases in humans come from animals (are zoonotic)?
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: The UN Environment Programme's 2020 report: about 60% of known infectious diseases and 75% of emerging ones are zoonotic.

questions.ask: Which of these does the UN Environment Programme list among the main drivers of new zoonotic diseases?
questions.answer: Increased demand for animal protein and intensive, unsustainable farming
distractors: Increased consumption of pulses and grains
questions.explain: They are two of seven human-caused drivers. Others include wildlife exploitation, travel, changing food supply chains and climate change.

questions.ask: Roughly how many people did the 2009 swine flu (H1N1) pandemic kill worldwide in its first year?
questions.explain: A modelling study led by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated 151,700–575,400 deaths. 80% were people under 65.

questions.ask: In which animals did the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus originate?
questions.explain: Genetic analysis traced the virus to swine in Mexico (Mena et al., eLife, 2016).

questions.ask: Of the human H5N1 bird flu cases reported to the World Health Organization since 2003, roughly what share were fatal?
questions.explain: 1,005 cases and 479 deaths in 25 countries from 2003 to October 2026. Mild cases often go unreported, so say 'about half of reported cases'.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of all antimicrobials sold worldwide are used in animals raised for food?
sourceDistractors: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 2015
questions.explain: Van Boeckel et al. (Science, 2019): 73% of antimicrobials sold globally are used in food animals.

questions.ask: Roughly how many deaths were directly caused by antibiotic-resistant infections worldwide in 2021?
questions.explain: The Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance Project (The Lancet, 2024): 1.14 million direct deaths in 2021, and 4.71 million in which resistance played a part. This covers all resistance, not just farming's share.

questions.ask: How many deaths are antibiotic-resistant infections forecast to cause directly between 2025 and 2050?
questions.explain: Without further action, direct deaths are forecast to total 39 million from 2025 to 2050, reaching 1.91 million a year.

questions.ask: Between 2000 and 2018 in low- and middle-income countries, what happened to the share of antibiotics that fail more than half the time in chickens and pigs?
questions.explain: From 0.15 to 0.41 in chickens and 0.13 to 0.34 in pigs (Van Boeckel et al., 2019).

questions.ask: What share of reporting countries still use antimicrobials to make farm animals grow faster?
questions.explain: The World Organisation for Animal Health's 2023 report: 41 of 157 countries. Global use in animals fell 13% between 2017 and 2019.

questions.ask: Is it accurate to say 'antibiotics on farms kill over a million people a year'?
questions.answer: No: the 1.14 million deaths are from all antibiotic resistance, of which farm use is one driver
distractors: Yes: all resistance comes from farms
Yes: the figure counts farm-linked deaths only
No: resistance has not caused any deaths
questions.explain: Overuse in human medicine is a major cause too. Say farm overuse is 'one of the drivers' of resistance.

questions.ask: Counting the whole food system (farming, land clearing, processing, transport, retail and waste), roughly what share of global greenhouse gas emissions does food cause?
questions.explain: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's 2025 brief puts agrifood systems at 16.5 Gt CO₂eq in 2023, 32% of global emissions. Crippa et al. (2021) independently found 34% for 2015.

questions.ask: Which boundary gives the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) figure of about 22% of global emissions?
questions.answer: AFOLU: agriculture, forestry & other land use
distractors: The whole food system, including supply chains
questions.explain: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (Working Group III) found AFOLU produced 22% of global emissions in 2019. It covers farming plus land use (mainly deforestation), but not processing, transport or retail.

questions.ask: Counting only farm-gate emissions (crop and livestock production and on-farm energy), what share of global emissions is that?
questions.explain: Farm gate was 8.1 Gt CO₂eq of the food system's 16.5 Gt in 2023, which works out to ~16% of global emissions. 32% is the whole food system, not the farm gate.

questions.ask: Which component makes up the largest part of food-system emissions?
questions.explain: In 2023: farm gate 8.1 Gt (49%), supply chain 5.2 Gt (32%), land-use change 3.2 Gt (19%).

questions.ask: The food system's share of global emissions fell from 38% (2001) to 32% (2023). What happened to its actual emissions over that period?
questions.explain: The share fell only because other sectors grew faster. Food-system emissions rose 21% between 2001 and 2023.

questions.ask: Roughly how do livestock's greenhouse gas emissions compare with those of all the world's data centres (including AI)?
distractors: Data centres emit about twice as much
questions.explain: Livestock: ~6,200 Mt CO₂eq a year (FAO, 2023). Data centres: ~180 Mt CO₂ (International Energy Agency, 2025). That's ~34×, or ~24× counting only on-farm livestock emissions.

questions.ask: About how much CO₂ do all the world's data centres emit per year from their electricity use?
questions.answer: About 180 million tonnes (~0.5% of energy CO₂)
questions.explain: The International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (2025) puts data centres at ~180 Mt CO₂, about 0.5% of combustion emissions, rising to ~1% by 2030 in its base case.

questions.ask: How does the emissions saving from a global switch to plant-based diets compare with shutting down every data centre?
questions.answer: The diet switch saves roughly 35–40 times more
distractors: Shutting down data centres saves more
The diet switch saves about twice as much
questions.explain: A plant-based world cuts ~6,600 Mt CO₂eq (Poore & Nemecek, 2018). All data centres emit ~180 Mt CO₂ (IEA, 2025). That's ~37×.

questions.ask: Roughly how does the irrigation and drinking water (blue water) consumed for animal products compare with all data centres' total water consumption?
questions.answer: Animal products use a few hundred times more
distractors: Animal products use about 5 times more
questions.explain: Animal products' blue water is ~151 km³ a year (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012). Data centres consume ~0.56 km³, including water for their electricity (IEA). That's ~270×.

questions.ask: Of data centres' total water consumption, roughly what share is direct cooling water?
questions.answer: About a quarter (most is water used to generate their electricity)
questions.explain: Of ~560 billion litres in 2023, ~140 billion was direct (cooling) and ~373 billion indirect (electricity generation). The rest was chip and hardware manufacturing.

questions.ask: According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) latest life-cycle estimate, what share of all human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock?
questions.explain: The FAO's 2023 Pathways report gives 6.2 Gt CO₂eq, about 12% of global emissions (reference year 2015). Avoid '51%': it comes from a non-peer-reviewed 2009 magazine article.

questions.ask: What was the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) earlier, widely quoted 2013 estimate of livestock's share of global emissions?
questions.explain: Gerber et al. (FAO, 2013, reference year 2005) estimated 7.1 Gt CO₂eq, 14.5%. FAO's current figure is 12%. The methods changed, and the drop doesn't mean emissions fell.

questions.ask: What share of global food-production emissions comes from animal-based foods?
questions.explain: Xu et al. (Nature Food, 2021) found animal-based foods produce 57% of food-production emissions and plant-based foods 29%. Beef alone accounts for 25%.

questions.ask: Meat and dairy produce over half of food's emissions. What share of the world's calories do they provide?
questions.explain: Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018): meat and dairy provide 18% of calories and 37% of protein, but use 83% of farmland.

questions.ask: Which animals account for the largest share of livestock emissions?
questions.explain: FAO (2023): cattle cause over 60% of livestock emissions, mostly from enteric methane. Pigs are ~15% and chickens ~9%.

questions.ask: Where does the often-repeated claim that livestock cause '51% of global emissions' come from?
questions.answer: A 2009 World Watch magazine article that was not peer-reviewed
distractors: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report
The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) 2023 Pathways report
A 2018 study in the journal Science
questions.explain: Goodland & Anhang (2009) published it in World Watch magazine, and the film Cowspiracy popularised it. It's widely criticised, so use FAO's 12% instead.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of the fresh water withdrawn from rivers, lakes and aquifers worldwide is used by agriculture?
questions.explain: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) 2025 AQUASTAT snapshot puts agriculture at 72% of freshwater withdrawals, industry at 15% and municipal use at 13%.

questions.ask: What share of global freshwater withdrawals goes to municipal use (homes and services)?
questions.explain: Municipal use is about 13% and industry 15%. Agriculture takes 72%, so diet matters far more for water than shower length.

questions.ask: Counting rainwater used by crops and the water needed to dilute pollution, what share of humanity's total water footprint comes from agriculture?
questions.explain: Hoekstra & Mekonnen (PNAS, 2012) found agriculture accounts for 92% of the global water footprint of 9,087 billion m³ a year (1996–2005).

questions.ask: In water-footprint accounting, what is 'green water'?
questions.answer: Rainwater stored in the soil and used by plants
distractors: Water taken from rivers and aquifers for irrigation
questions.explain: Green = rainwater in the soil. Blue = surface and groundwater (irrigation). Grey = the water needed to dilute pollution to safe levels.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of agriculture's total water footprint (rainwater, irrigation and pollution combined) goes to producing animal products?
questions.explain: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (Ecosystems, 2012) found 29% of agriculture's water footprint is for animal products. Counting all water on grazing land, Weindl et al. (2017) get 56%.

questions.ask: What kind of water makes up most of the water footprint of animal production?
questions.answer: Rainwater (green water) used by feed crops and pasture: ~87%
distractors: Irrigation water from rivers and aquifers
Water used in slaughterhouses and processing
questions.explain: Of 2,422 billion m³ a year, 87% is green (rain), 7% grey (pollution) and 6% blue (irrigation and drinking). Drinking water is a tiny part.

questions.ask: Counting all water used on grazing land, what share of agricultural water consumption is linked to livestock?
questions.explain: Weindl et al. (Global Environmental Change, 2017) estimate livestock-related water is 56% of agricultural water consumption, when all water on grazing land is counted.

questions.ask: Counting only irrigation (blue) water, roughly what share of agriculture's water footprint goes to animal products?
questions.explain: Calculated from Mekonnen & Hoekstra's figures: 151 of ~945 billion m³ of agricultural blue water. Most irrigation water goes to crops people eat directly, like rice and wheat.

questions.ask: Drinking and servicing water for farm animals is roughly what share of global freshwater use?
questions.explain: Drinking water is tiny (~0.6%, cited in Weindl et al., 2017). Livestock's water is almost all embedded in feed.

questions.ask: Per calorie, roughly how much larger is beef's water footprint than that of cereals and starchy roots?
questions.explain: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (Ecosystems, 2012): the average water footprint per calorie for beef is 20 times that of cereals and starchy roots.

questions.ask: Per gram of protein, how does meat's water footprint compare with that of pulses (beans, lentils, peas)?
questions.explain: Chicken is at the low end (~1.5×) and beef at the high end (~6×). Even for protein, plants need much less water.

questions.ask: What is the global average water footprint (green + blue + grey) of 1 kg of beef?
questions.explain: About 15,000 L/kg for beef, compared with ~6,000 for pork and ~4,300 for chicken. Most of it is rainwater on feed and pasture, so don't imply it all comes from taps or rivers.

questions.ask: Why do animal foods have larger water footprints than plant foods of the same nutritional value?
questions.answer: Animals convert only a small share of their feed into food, and the feed needs water to grow
distractors: Animals drink very large amounts of water
Slaughterhouses use most of the water
questions.explain: It's feed conversion. Drinking water is a tiny share (~0.6% of global freshwater use); the water is embedded in the feed.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of global deforestation is driven by agricultural expansion?
questions.explain: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) satellite survey (FRA 2020 Remote Sensing Survey, published 2022) found agricultural expansion drove almost 90% of global deforestation in 2000–2018.

questions.ask: According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) satellite survey, what share of global deforestation was caused by livestock grazing (2000–2018)?
questions.explain: Livestock grazing caused 38.5% and cropland expansion (incl. oil palm) almost 50%. Together, agriculture drove almost 90%.

questions.ask: Which single commodity is the biggest driver of tropical deforestation?
distractors: Soy for tofu and soy milk
questions.explain: Pendrill et al. (2019), summarised by Our World in Data: cattle pasture caused ~41% of tropical deforestation, more than all oilseeds (soy and palm oil) combined (~18%).

questions.ask: What share of the world's soy is eaten directly by people as tofu, soy milk, tempeh or edamame?
questions.explain: Only ~7% of soy is eaten as tofu, soy milk, tempeh or edamame. 77% is fed to livestock (2018 data, Fraanje & Garnett via Our World in Data).

questions.ask: What share of tropical deforestation is driven directly or indirectly by agriculture?
questions.explain: Pendrill et al. (Science, 2022): 90–99% of tropical deforestation is agriculture-driven, but only 45–65% of cleared land goes into active production.

questions.ask: If the world removed meat and dairy from diets, by roughly how much could global farmland use fall?
questions.explain: Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018) found farmland could fall by more than 75% while still feeding the world.

questions.ask: The farmland that a plant-based world could free up is roughly equivalent to the area of:
questions.answer: The USA, China, the EU and Australia combined
questions.explain: About 3.1 billion hectares, equal to the USA, China, the EU and Australia combined.

questions.ask: In a plant-based world, what would happen to the area of cropland (not just grazing land)?
questions.answer: It would also fall, because feed crops would no longer be needed
distractors: It would need to roughly double
It would stay exactly the same
It would rise slightly to replace meat
questions.explain: Feed crops take a large share of cropland, and animals convert feed to food inefficiently. Growing food for people directly needs less cropland, not more.

questions.ask: Per 100 g of protein, roughly how much more land does beef (from beef herds) need than peas?
questions.explain: About 164 m² for beef vs 3.4 m² for peas per 100 g of protein, about 48×.

questions.ask: How does the lowest-impact beef compare with peas for land use per unit of protein?
questions.answer: It still uses about 36 times more land
distractors: It uses less land than peas
It uses about the same land
It uses about twice the land
questions.explain: Even the lowest-impact beef uses ~36× more land and causes ~6× more greenhouse gases than peas. Grass-fed doesn't close the gap.

questions.ask: Per 100 g of protein, which of these uses the MOST land?
questions.explain: Lamb (~185 m²) and beef from beef herds (~164 m²) are far above everything else. Pig meat is ~11 m², poultry ~7.1 m² and nuts ~7.9 m².

questions.ask: Per 100 g of protein, roughly how much land does poultry meat need compared with peas?
questions.explain: Poultry is ~7.1 m² and peas ~3.4 m² per 100 g of protein. Chicken is much more land-efficient than beef, but still about 2× peas.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of the world's farmland (grazing land plus cropland for feed) is used for livestock?
questions.explain: Our World in Data (Ritchie & Roser), using UN Food and Agriculture Organization data, puts livestock at ~80% of agricultural land. Poore & Nemecek (2018) give 83%.

questions.ask: Livestock use most of the world's farmland. Roughly what share of the world's calories do meat, dairy and farmed fish supply?
questions.explain: Meat, dairy and farmed fish supply ~17% of calories and ~38% of protein, while using ~80% of farmland.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of the world's habitable land (excluding glaciers and deserts) is used for agriculture?
questions.explain: 44% of habitable land is farmed (an older version of the chart said 50%). Habitable land excludes glaciers (~10% of land) and barren land (~14%).

questions.ask: How is the world's agricultural land roughly split between grazing land and cropland?
questions.explain: About two-thirds of agricultural land is grazing land. Of the remaining third (cropland), a large part grows animal feed.
